speechtext:
The House resumed from Thursday, September 15, consideration of Bill C-144, an Act to authorize payments by Canada toward the provision of child care services, and to amend the Canada Assistance Plan in consequence thereof, as reported (with amendments) from a legislative committee; and the amendments of Ms. Mitchell:
Motion No. 36
That Bill C-144 be amended by deleting Clause 10.
Motion No. 38
That Bill C-144 be amended by deleting Clause 11.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Continuing debate with the Hon. Member for Churchill.

Mr. Speaker, again it is an honour to get up in the House and speak on child care which we believe is a national priority for all Canadians. In my riding I think one of the things that we have to be concerned about is making sure that we increase the availability of child care for people in remote communities.
One of the concerns that we have with the legislation that is in front of us is that because it lacks national standards, national objectives, that will be followed through, we are not sure if we will have these day care centres and available spaces in the communities that need them. I would like to spend a few minutes in talking about why that is essential.
In native populations we have high unemployment. Among native women we have higher unemployment. It is essential that we increase not only the job opportunities for those women but also the opportunities for those women to get training. One of the ways that that can happen is if we are in a situation in which those women and those families are guaranteed adequate child care. That is not difficult, but it is not that hard either if the Government has the political will to make it happen.
We would like to see within the legislation that we have before us some means of increasing funding for child care to increase the spaces that are available. I noticed yesterday that
the Minister tried to ridicule the amendment put forward by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Vancouver East (Ms. Mitchell). That is not surprising, since the Minister has ridiculed everybody who has an opinion different from his own on this issue. He does not have to listen just to my learned colleague, the Hon. Member for Vancouver East. He could have listened to the various groups that have made presentations to the House of Commons committee. They were concerned with the same issue that my colleague was concerned about. It is interesting to note that all 40 groups that came forward at the committee hearings spoke against the Government's project.
There would have been more people speaking against the Government's project if government Members on that committee had not limited the hearings to two days of investigation. It was two days on a child care program that is supposed to be national in scope, an issue which is so controversial, so important. This Government says two days is enough to study it, two days is enough for groups across Canada to make their presentations.
1 always considered it a problem with this Government that when something is controversial it does not want it studied. When something is important, whether it is trade, child care, or tax reform, it wants to limit public input.
It reminds me of that leaked government document a couple of years ago where they wanted to low profile the trade issue. They did not want it to become a public issue. We know why. We see with the recent polls that the more Canadians know about this Prime Minister's trade deal with the American President the more they dislike it.
The same situation would exist with child care. The Minister, his officials, his cabinet colleagues, and backbenchers, those who were not promoted to Cabinet yesterday, have all gone out and said what a wonderful program it is, how it provides the money for stay home mothers-80 cents a day, I understand-and how that is really helping our young children across this nation. As those kinds of facts become public more and more people will know that we are getting another flim-flam from this Government.
Four years after the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) promised that we would have child care legislation, they finally come up with this package. They want to rush it through the House of Commons, not because they believe it is a priority

September 16, 1988
Canada Child Care Act
but because there might be an election in the next couple of weeks. They want to keep one or two promises in the whole area of social policies even if it is a flim-flam, even if it is done at the last possible moment, and even if it is not meeting the concerns of people across Canada including the people in the remote communities that I mentioned in opening my remarks.
Specifically on the amendment put forward by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Vancouver East, we believe that the amendment put forward is the type of thing that we need to improve this legislation.
Yesterday the Government accepted a motion that would finally make it possible for concerned groups to have access to the arrangements made with each of the provinces and what would be in those arrangements. We had an amendment put forward and eventually accepted by this House that would ensure the public access to those agreements and to any amended version of those agreements. That was important.
More important, we must make sure that there is adequate funding. The intent of this amendment by the Hon. Member for Vancouver East and of the other amendments she has put forward in the same area is to increase funding for child care spaces and to make sure that the Government's legislation does not actually limit the number of spaces which will be created over the next number of years.
1 indicated earlier that a number of groups have spoken specifically on that point. In their presentations to the House of Commons committee they indicated that they would support that type of amendment. I will just read from three of the briefs that were presented to this committee. I am taking a cross-section because, as the Hon. Member for Vancouver East has indicated, approximately 40 groups spoke against this legislation in committee. Many of them spoke on this specific aspect of the legislation. I will start by taking the presentation of one union group, the National Union of Provincial Government Employees, which said:
I'm sure all of you here tonight remember what constituted a "subsidized space" in childcare-funding-parlance in the days before the National Childcare Strategy. BNCS we had CAP, and in CAP language a "subsidized" space meant a space which was available for the child of a low-income family at a subsidized fee.
In fact, when the National Childcare Strategy was unveiled in late 1987, and the Minister and departmental officials talked glowingly of 200,000 new childcare spaces, "most of which would be subsidized", even those of us who have been keenly involved in the childcare policy debate long enough to consider ourselves veterans failed at first to grasp that the federal government had written a new dictionary of childcare language.
We continued to think that a subsidized space was a subsidized space, and we had great difficulty figuring out how the Government could claim to be funding 200,000 new subsidized spaces on the allocations of direct funding outlined in the National Strategy.
Now, of course, we've been re-educated on the subject of what the government means when it talks about a "subsidized space". In the era after the National Strategy on Childcare, a subsidized space is merely a space for which a province, having received money from the federal government, provides a "meaningful subsidy". "Meaningful subsidy", in the new federal childcare dictionary is currently defined as $2/space/day. At $2/space/day, the new subsidized space is much cheaper for governments than the old CAP definition of a subsidized space, which might range as high as $27 for a space filled by a toddler from a low-income family.
After looking at the legislation, at what the Government was doing, one group realized that it would indeed limit the contributions of the federal Government in this area. It was not the only group that made presentations, as I mentioned earlier.
We also have the brief of the the National Anti-Poverty Organization which, in part said: "Under existing cost-sharing agreements, child care has been funded as part of the Canada Assistance Plan. One of its components is social services that are eligible for cost-sharing if they serve those in need or those likely to be in need without the service. This objective is indeed clear. While the money has been removed from this program to provide funds for the Canada Child Care Act, its objectives have neither been replicated nor replaced in this Bill". It went on to say: "Removing the funds for cost-sharing child care from the Canada Assistance Plan to the Canada Child Care Act accomplished several federal Government goals", but not necessarily doing what it should do to help low-income Canadians. That is why the National Anti-Poverty Organization has spoken out against this legislation.
Further, the Government's own Canadian Advisory Council on the Status of Women, people appointed by the Prime Minister and his Cabinet, has also come out in its brief against what the Government is doing. In this specific area of the amendment put forward by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Vancouver East, it said that the Government had actually moved backward.
To read part of its brief in the few minutes that I have remaining, it said:
In 1973, 15 years ago, the Council pointed out the "evident inability of the federal-provincial governments to come to grips with the problem of child care services so urgently needed in Canada." In 1986, we reiterated our belief that "child care ... is an essential service which should be universally accessible."
The Canada Assistance Plan (CAP) was one solution; Bill C-144 is another. However, neither of them acknowledge that child care, for low-income and middle-class families alike, will become part of the Canadian landscape; that families cannot bear this burden without considerable help; and that that help must intelligently, in good faith, and with the most intense political will, come from a government that has the foresight to understand that the labour force requires the participation of women and men, and that responsible fiscal planning for the future requires a great commitment for the care of our children.
What I am trying to point out-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I will let the Hon. Member wind up.

Mr. Speaker, I thank you for the extra few seconds, and I certainly will not abuse it. What I am trying to point out from the briefs that I have scanned in terms of what I have said this morning is that it is not only our amendment that we are speaking to in the House of Commons. What we are speaking to is a belief widely held by groups across this country that this child care legislation is not doing what it should be.
September 16, 1988

Again through the use of flimflammery the Government has actually restricted the ability to provide the child care services that are needed across this country. It is not just our belief, and the Minister may not like our amendments, it is what people across this country have been saying in front of the committee in the two brief days that the Government would allow the public to make presentations.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak on this very important amendment. I am very concerned about the fact that the so-called child care strategy brought to the House is one that eliminates people who normally would be able to have some access to child care.
I must say the people, certainly the children, and the families of Canada, are very fortunate that they have had a Member of Parliament such as the Hon. Member for Vancouver East (Ms. Mitchell) who really understands child care. I am very concerned about a Government that will bring forward a Bill that states that this is a child care strategy. What it is really doing is demeaning the ability to deliver child care in our country.
Anyone who has children would start to understand that, first of all, we are looking at children in need and we are looking at children of low-income families who, if the provinces use this Bill, will be cut off in the Canada Assistance Plan. That is really important. We have looked at the statistics and the analysis. We recognize that if the Canada Assistance Plan was left in place at least these people would have access to the kind of quality care that is available to them at the moment.
Second, what we have done with this is said to people who already have spaces, regardless of what kind of spaces they have, that they will be able to get tax exemptions. That is not what we are looking for. We are looking at two million children out there in need of care. Certainly the New Democratic Party has recognized for a long time that to make sure families are secure and have a basis of choice they must have the services that are there. Suggesting that this is something that we cannot afford in Canada is saying that we cannot afford to give stability and caring to families and children. That is not the position of New Democratic Party.
In the Minister's comments yesterday he stated that he was not going to implement the Meech Lake principles. This Government said that it was at last going to be able to establish national standards, but he did not want to do this for children. Again it is this flop-flop that the Government is using. Children are not important to the Government. It is about time that it recognized that the people of Canada do care about their children.
We are looking at a program that will cut off the Canada Assistance Plan that now is at least addressing the needs of low-income people. That plan will be cut off if they kick into this type of Act. That is unacceptable, it is unfair, and it certainly does not serve the children of Canada well.
Canada Child Care Act
There are many research institutions in this country and a lot of research has been done on child development. We have the information, and we know what is needed. We know that those first eight years are the most crucial years in any person's developmental stages, yet the Government is again saying that it is not going to worry about it. Every research institute that looked at child care has said "eliminate the welfare system network for child care and put it into a national child care strategy so all children will be seen as equals, at least for those first eight years". No matter what they have to face in life later on, at least they will be given that base.
What the Government has done in putting this Act in place is discriminating against the low-income people and the people who normally would be able to be part of that welfare assistance plan. The research institutes and the New Democratic Party have stated that if we are going to put a national strategy in place, get that national strategy in place. In the meantime there has to be a phasing in so that the low-income people and the children in real need have the ability to use that Canada Assistance Plan.
This Government has turned down two amendments that would have helped to be put that in place. We have an amendment in front of us this morning that is really saying "allow that to happen", Mr. Speaker, to assist the children who are homeless, the children who are of the working poor, and the families that are under pressure in their existence because of poverty.
It is all very well for the Government to brag about the kinds of programs it has put in place that have actually given assistance to those who already have money, who have places for their child care, and who are comfortable when they go to work knowing that their children are well looked after and that they can afford to pay for it. Is that the kind of society this Government wants to be part of, a society that builds two Canadas, a Canada for the children of those who have the ability to be able to pay for their child care, independent of any help from society, except extra tax exemptions? Rather, do we want to a build a society that says a child born in this country is a valuable treasure, a person that we understand has the potential of being a very productive and secure and creative individual in our country?
As a Party we know that investing in children is probably the most serious and important investment we can make in all times. As New Democrats we understand that if we are going to build a base of a secure society we must build that base in the first eight years of a child's life. If we want families to be able to operate with some security, with knowing that they can build their family unity together with a sense of security that their children will be well looked after and safe, then we need a child care program that does not discriminate against the children in need.

September 16, 1988
Canada Child Care Act
Many, many briefs were put forward to the committee. They were briefs from people who were not necessarily seen as supporting the New Democratic Party, but they were briefs from people who had done an analysis of this Child Care Act. Every one of those briefs objected to the Bill that we have in front of us and said that it is bad, withdraw it, leave the status quo rather than put something in that will really threaten the quality of care that our children are presently getting.
We know there has been a crisis in Canada in child care. We know there have been people who have been on long waiting lists for years. We know that there are certain provinces where it is almost impossible to get any kind of quality care. Yet with all of that, these people who have studied the Act have said leave the status quo the way it is, rather than implement this, because it is increasing the discrimination against people of lower income and certainly the working poor. It is also saying that we have no guarantee of any quality care in this country.
They really are not going to put in any national objectives that say that whether one is in Newfoundland, in British Columbia, in the Yukon, or in the Northwest Territories, a child in Canada has a right to specific kinds of quality care. There is nothing in the Bill that addresses that, and the Minister is saying that he chose to ignore the fact that at least in Meech Lake we are allowed to start to put in national objectives. However, he wants to ignore that, and says quite blatantly that he has ignored the fact that national objectives are possible in Meech Lake. He does not intend to implement them. That is a fine way to be responsible about what child care is all about.
Every one of us here, men, women, and parents who understand what that basic need is for children, cannot in any conscience support this Bill and not support these amendments. Surely, we have to look at the implications for the children of the working poor and the low-income families in Canada. What we are doing is relegating them to an adult life of trauma, because this Parliament is not willing to use the resources of this very rich country to say that children are important, and because this Government has a majority it is being crassly ignorant of the needs of children.
Members opposite stand up and talk about this child care strategy. It is not a child care strategy at all. It is just making it easy for people running private child care centres to increase their profit. Obviously the Government thinks that children are there for profit. Instead of looking at non-profit cooperative kinds of service delivery and recognizing that our children are a major resource, the Government refuses to accept an important amendment which would, at least for a time, extend a safety net to low-income families and poor children. It would give some sense of hope to families that are under so much stress from living in a society where they see many people with lots of resources while they are eking out an existence from day to day.
I see you giving me a sign that my time is up, Mr. Speaker. I will respect that, but I certainly hope the Government will review what it is doing to the future of this country and our families and children when it dares to bring in an Act such as this.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom).

Mr. Speaker, your French is getting better every day but the accent is still Edmonton!

I wanted to say a few words about the Child Care Act before the House today. As you know, Mr. Speaker, I come from a rural riding in Saskatchewan with many different communities. It contains about 10,000 or 15,000 farmers. It has about 60 different villages and small towns and hamlets and a couple of very small cities. The Minister himself, coming from a very similar riding in Manitoba, should understand that there are some very particular needs and concerns, some special problems with respect to child care in rural Manitoba. However, I do not think this Bill addresses those needs.
We need more flexibility to provide funding to parents' groups, co-operatives, community associations, in order to provide decent child care in rural Canada. It must be a lot more flexible because we are dealing with small hamlets, villages, and towns. In addition, we have many farms scattered over many miles of rural Canada. There are parts of my riding where you can go for a mile or two from farm to farm, and then you get down to southern Saskatchewan or southern Alberta and you can go for five or ten miles from one farm to a ranch or another farm. The problem of child care is a different problem in rural Canada from what it is in urban Canada. I do not think this Bill takes into account the need for flexibility across rural Canada.
In rural Canada on the farm problems arise because of a given season. I am thinking of the harvest season which is just winding up in my area. That is a special problem. There are many farms that do not need or want child care on a full-time basis, but do need it on a part-time basis for the harvest season or during spring planting. It is then a necessity.
Neither is it just for the male farmer. The woman farmer is a 100 per cent participant in planting and harvesting crops. Therefore, I hope the Minister, being from rural Canada and representing a riding very similar to mine, would be more open to suggestions and amendments to make this legislation even better.

Mr. Speaker, I know I was not on the committee that examined this legislation, but I know that over 40 witnesses appeared before the Committee last week, and our Member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell) was there.
September 16, 1988

Everybody present was opposed to the legislation, Mr. Speaker. Everybody was against it. Only two days were allowed to hear witnesses here in Ottawa and give them a chance to express their views and opinions on this Bill. If everybody was against the legislation, I wonder why the Government did not propose any amendments. This is a democracy, Mr. Speaker, and public opinion is very important in Canada. On the other hand, the Government spent $15 million last year on public opinion polls. A lot of money was spent because Allan Gregg and recently, a couple of Senators, wanted to sound out public opinion. I hope the Minister will be in the House very shortly. There were 40 witnesses, and after two days, everybody was opposed to this Bill. So why didn't the Minister propose any amendments to introduce changes in the Bill?

I really wonder why, after two days of hearings and over 40 witnesses against this legislation, there is not an amendment that will take into account what those witnesses want. Surely that is the democratic system. Surely that is the purpose of public hearings.
In the two or three minutes that remain I want to place on the record an example of what I am speaking about. Perhaps the Minister will respond. Over 40 witnesses appeared before the committee last week and I am told every one of them opposed the legislation. The Minister had a reputation as someone who would listen to the people of Canada. I wonder why he is now proposing amendments that go against the beliefs of those who appeared as witnesses. I have here, for example, a copy of the brief from the Canadian Jewish Congress presented to the legislative committee on September 8.
It says: "The concern with replacing the Canada Assistance Plan lies in the fact that while it was flawed in its child care funding mechanism, it at least afforded protection to low-income users". It goes on to say that this entitlement to subsidies for low-income earners is now negotiable in federal-provincial arrangements and may effectively disappear under the new system, hurting the people least able to afford good care. It also says that it is uncertain whether the provinces will be able to maintain the same level of low-income subsidization in addition to the new competing interests that are there. This may make it extremely difficult for a province to continue providing CAP style low and middle-income family subsidies while providing grants to a variety of meaningfully subsidized child care programs. This may be the case particularly after the seventh year of the program when matching operating cost funding is curtailed and capital cost funding ceases.
That is what the Congress says in its in its brief that goes on for eight or nine pages. It expresses, on behalf of the people it represents, concern about the Minister's legislation.
I also have a copy of the brief submitted by members of the Canadian Union of Public Employees. They, too, are really concerned about the kind of amendment the Minister is
Canada Child Care Act
turning down. They say: "The Canadian Union of Public Employees sincerely and passionately believes that it was a sad day indeed for parents and children and child care providers when Bill C-144 was introduced into the House. To be blunt, we think the enactment of this legislation would represent a callous and backward act by an insensitive government".
Those are pretty tough words, "callous and insensitive government", but truer words have never been spoken. Over 40 witnesses came before the committee, and the Minister will sit there and not listen. What is democracy all about? What is the parliamentary system all about if the Minister will not respond to the wishes of the people? What are we all about if we do not respond? The Minister will not even bring in amendments to make sure there are national objectives in place despite the fact that this Parliament passed the Meech Lake Accord last year which says we can now have national objectives for programs like day care.
This is one of the first opportunities we have had to enact the spirit of Meech Lake, and the Minister himself was an eloquent critic. He was a good critic in the Opposition on the constitutional proposal back in 1981-82. If there is any Minister who understands that proposition, it is the Minister in charge of health and welfare. Yet he is not responding when he has a golden opportunity.

Mr. Speaker, in concluding, since my 10 minutes are up, I want to say that it is time to act. It is time to do something for Canada's children and to do something concrete.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Is the House ready for the question?
Question.

Mr. Speaker, I think not. I think the House is not yet ready for the question. We are ready to face the issue head on.
I have been spending the last couple weeks in my riding knocking on doors, talking to people, and I have found that Manitobans, the people in Winnipeg and the people in Winnipeg North Centre, are interested in issues, contrary to the mythology that people are only interested in personalities, in whether or not the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) has a smile on his face. The people are not only interested in style, they are interested in issues.
Two issues are uppermost in the minds of the people. One is the trade deal and the other is day care. These are important and fundamental issues that people across Canada are concerned about. The people tell me that they need day care, that there is not enough day care to give appropriate and proper care to their children. They have to work in order to make ends meet.

September 16, 1988
Canada Child Care Act
Increasing numbers of Canadians have to work at two jobs. It is no longer possible for a person to make a decent income on one salary; there has to be two salaries. When two parents are working out of necessity, the children must be taken care of properly and that creates a new demand for day care. This demand exists at the grass roots level. It must be responded to and it must be responded to in a substantive way.
I want to make a few comments about the Government's day care program. Having examined this program, I find it is more propaganda than substance. It is more sleight of hand than it is day care spaces. It is more flimsy than reality. This program fails in some fundamental ways. It fails to meet the needs of the women and the families in my riding and in all the ridings across Canada. It fails to add sufficiently and significantly to the number of spaces in Canada. What Canadian families need is day care spaces so that our children get appropriate care.
This is a propaganda program. It was a propaganda announcement that the Government made. In fact, it is not only a propaganda gesture, it is an inept one. I would have expected more of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp).
What do I mean when I say that this is an inept propaganda gesture? The Tories made a big announcement of $6 billion, and they caught the headlines. Of course, when the people read below the headlines, when they read the full story of day care, they find out something which is often true. The headlines differ from the story.
With this new Conservative day care program, a ceiling is put on the amount of money going into day care. Up until now, under the Canada Assistance Plan, day care spaces were expanding at the rate of 15 per cent per year. Under this new program, day care spaces will be expanding at what rate? They will be expanding at the rate of 10 per cent per year. Ten per cent is less than 15 per cent and any person with a little arithmetic understands that.
This program is retarding the growth of day care. It is putting off the day when the needs of the ordinary Canadian family for the proper care of children will be met. That is the first way in which this program is a deception.
Another significant way it is a deception is that this program weakens the commitment to providing day care for the poor. 1 want to back up what I have said with the statements of some groups that have analysed this matter. The Canadian Day Care Advocacy Association says the following in its brief:
Bill C-144 is silent on the definition of a "subsidized space". It is the federal Government's responsibility to see that all subsidized spaces-existing spaces as well as the "200,000" new spaces-are adequately funded in terms of individual family's financial needs. By that, we mean that existing spaces should continue to be funded at no less than their current level. It is common knowledge that the new definition, a "subsidized space" could be a space that receives as little as $2.00 a day of public funds. We find that unacceptable, because it would leave such spaces out of the reach of low and middle-income Canadians. The "space count" should not leave room for this kind of exclusion.
The Canadian Day Care Advocacy Association is saying that this new program leaves out the poor. It is heartless and it
runs the danger of providing less day care for the poor in Canada. The Canadian Federation of Students said the following:
The fact that there are no guaranteed subsidies for low-income Canadians is of great concern to us. Student parents in need of child care are low-income Canadians. The subsidies that are in place under the Canada Assistance Plan should, at the very least, be guaranteed under the new Canada Child Care Act. As this is not the case, the Canada Assistance Plan represents a "safer" option for low-income Canadians. We would parenthetically add here that the income tax provisions under the national childcare strategy will not be of much use to students. Most students will not need the deductions and the additional child credits are too little, and too long after the refund would be of use.
Members of the Canadian Federation of Students indicate that the Canada Assistance Plan is a better plan for them than the new Tory plan. In the opinion of the Canadian Federation of Students, this is a step backward rather than a step forward.
The National Council of Women of Canada says the following:
Our first problem with this new bill is that it does not seem to ensure that the supply of these spaces will increase, indeed there seems even to be the danger that they might decrease, because while under the Canada Assistance Plan support for such spaces for low income families is open-ended to meet needs as identified, under the new Act, there will be a ceiling. A fixed cost-shared federal contribution will be available to provinces on a yearly basis, for a variety of purposes including capital funding, operating and grants etc. but without specific reference to subsidy needs. Our concern is that impoverished families may lose out.
The Government ought to be moving forward with care, with heart, trying to include all Canadians under its umbrella. What in fact the National Council of Women of Canada, the Canadian Federation of Students, and the Canadian Day Care Advocacy Association have said is that this program puts in jeopardy the day care spaces that are available for the poor. That is a major indictment of this program. The program is a step backward rather than a step forward.
There are two points about the substance of this program that are fundamental. The Government's new plan reduces the increase in spaces and therefore is a step backward. It threatens the subsidies for the poor and is therefore a step backward.
I see you indicating that I have two minutes left, Mr. Speaker. I just want to make this point. Over the last decade or two our society has changed significantly. No longer do the vast majority of women stay home and look after children. In today's society women who stay home and look after their children are in the minority. In my family that is the case, but my family is in the minority. The reality for the majority of families these days is that both parents have to work to make ends meet, both parents are in the market-place, and we have to ensure adequate care for the children.
If we are going to have a great nation in the future, if our children are going to be able to meet their responsibilities in the future, they need adequate care today. The Government was challenged to move in and meet that need, and it has
September 16, 1988

failed abysmally. It has the headlines, but when we read the story under the headlines we find a program that is a step backward rather than a step forward. That is why I say this program is more propaganda than substance. What ordinary Canadian families in my riding have been asking me for, as I have gone door to door to talk to them, is more day care spaces. They want a place in their neighbourhood at which their children can receive adequate care while they go to work.
I call upon the Government to rethink what it is doing. I call upon the Government to re-examine the critiques being made by this Party and the critiques of the National Council of Women, the Canadian Federation of Students, the Canadian Day Care Association, the Advocacy Association. The Government should rethink what it is doing, go back to the drawing board, and come up with a plan that will be a real step forward.
Mir. Jim Fulton (Skeena): Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity this morning to speak on Bill C-144, particularly on the amendment put forward by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Vancouver East (Ms. Mitchell), which would retain the participation of CAP, the Canadian Assistance Plan, in child care and day care. I see the Minister is here. I know a little about this field, having been a probation and parole officer and having been involved in the field of child care most of my professional life. I have in fact set up and been the president of a day care society. I did that 13 years ago in a small northern community in British Columbia.
I recognized then the rapidly evolving need for day care because of the increasing number of families where either both parents worked or, in the case of single parent families, where the single parent is very often involved in the workforce. In all cases, at least at some point during each day or each week, the parent is away from the child. I know something of the problems associated with day care and child care. I also know what the outcome is for many children where proper care is not provided. That is why I point out to the Minister that having been a probation and parole officer I recognize the problems that many children get into. Often one can find the root causes in terms of the care provided to them in their earliest years. I do not think there is anyone in this House who would dispute that the early years in the life of a child are key to the development of that child's personality throughout his or her life.
I want to spend a moment on the needs of northern child care and of child care among first nations, among native families, because that is an area of real crisis. I do not think the Government has addressed this problem at all. There are no objectives in Bill C-144 which are directly related to the amendment put forward by my friend the Hon. Member for Vancouver East. She has brought forward not only this amendment for us today, but also amendments over the last few days related to the need for objectives.
I am surprised after all the talk from the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and other Ministers that the Meech Lake
Canada Child Care Act
Accord did not have any kind of viral implant in terms of the potential for national legislation to have objectives. The Government was always planning to bring forward national programs that would have objectives, yet the very first time it has an opportunity to bring something forward we find there was a back room virus, at least among Tories, in relation to the Meech Lake Accord.
Obviously, every two facilities across the country are not going to be the same no matter what kind of objectives there are, but there are certain things one has to have for a safe protected environment for children. I think particularly of the training for those who will be working in this field. Having worked in the field myself I know what kind of training is required. My children are young, aged four and six years. I have some kind of idea of what kind of situations they feel best in, what kind of people they get along with best, what kind of toys and what kind of environment they need. Why would the Government not put those kinds of objectives clearly into a piece of legislation for those who are the most important in our society and in every society around the world? I can only assume that the Government never really intended to bring forward a plan to reach those hundreds of thousands of children in need of care during the day.
We know there are over two million children in Canada whose parents, either one or both, work and they are involved in some kind of care situation. It might be with a grandmother, a neighbour, or a licensed day care facility. All kinds of situations have evolved because the need is there. What Governments are supposed to do in collecting taxes is to spend the money in the most effective, rational, and cost-effective way.
Bill C-144 does not meet any of those criteria. That is why all groups that appeared before the committee last week oppose the Bill. Not some of them, not half of them, not three-quarters of them; all groups that appeared oppose the Bill. One would assume that the Minister or perhaps some of his backbenchers might have been able to find a group somewhere in Canada they could invite who would say that this was the next best thing to sliced bread, that this was what they always wanted. However, it would not be those who are knowledgeable about the needs of children, what kinds of facilities are required, or what kinds of capital funding are required.
The Minister's Bill provides for an ending to capital funding after seven years. The Minister crows that there are 200,000 licensed subsidized spaces and that it is going to double, that there will be 400,000 spaces seven years from now. As many groups across the country have pointed out that many spaces would be developed without the Bill, without the Minister's proposal.
I think we have to ask ourselves: What is this Bill, really? It appears to be, and it may well be, a sop to those who are not crucially involved in day care. When Tories are out knocking on doors they can say they brought forward this child care Bill.

CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-FORMER JUDGE'S ANALYSIS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, after reading the entire trade agreement, which is more than the Minister for International Trade (Mr. Crosbie) seems to have done, former Family Court Judge, Marjorie Bowker, wrote a thoughtful analysis of the agreement.
Her conclusions are worth putting on the record. They are as follows:
There can be no equality where one partner is the most powerful nation on earth, the other a subordinate on the world stage; one with a population of 260 million, the other with only 26 million. Unlike the European Economic Community, a union of 12 relatively equal nations, this is an unequal union- much like that between a walrus and a frog, an elephant and a mouse. Such an union can have but one result-the smaller being swallowed by the larger. .. What Canadians can ponder in the little time that remains, is not so much what the free trade agreement will do to certain sections of our economy, but rather what it will do to Canada as a whole-
Clearly the vision of Judge Bowker and that of the Government are light years apart. Her vision is the one to which the majority of Canadians would subscribe.

Mr. Speaker yesterday, on September 15, 1988, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) appointed a minister of forestry for Canada. Unfortunately, there is no national forest Act. In 1984 the Prime Minister promised that "a Progressive Conservative Government will recognize the vital importance of the industry by appointing a Minister of Forestry".
Recognition has meant a four-year wait. Vital importance has meant a 35 per cent export tax on shakes and shingles and 15 per cent export tax on softwood lumber. Vital importance means that nine out of 10 federal-provincial forest renewal agreements are about to run out, and the Cabinet has refused to give a mandate even to negotiate extensions. The forest sector employs over one million Canadians, the largest industry in Canada and our largest source of a positive balance of trade.
The Tories, prior to 1984, roundly condemned the Trudeau Liberals for returning less than 10 cents out of every dollar taxed from the forest sector to that sector for reforestation, research, and marketing. It is still less than 10 cents out of every dollar. No other industry is so regularly milked and given so little in return.
September 16, 1988

Mr. Speaker, I want to bring to the attention of the House a serious problem faced by the Dakota Tipi Reservation in the Portage Interlake area of Manitoba.
In 1985 they were approached by Special ARDA to establish an economic project dealing with the growth of seedlings that would be supplying reforestation projects in Manitoba. Private consultants were hired by Special ARDA to manage the program and over the past two or three years, because of what is clearly a case of mismanagement, the program failed. At the same time the Dakota Tipi Reservation was required to put in $80,000 of its own band money which it has not been able to recover.
The reason I raise it in the House today is that the band is yet unable to get Special ARDA to come to the table to talk about the problem. They have not been able to find anybody to negotiate or deal with the issues to find some kind of solution that would not put this reserve in jeopardy of bankruptcy at the risk of all the other social and economic programs supplied by the reserve.
I rise to my feet on behalf of the reserve hoping that the Ministers and officials of Special ARDA will take account of this very serious problem, respond to the band request, and see if they can find a resolution to the very serious difficulties in which the band members now find themselves.

Mr. Speaker, I rise at this moment also to complain about a lack of adequate funding from the federal Government for the native people in Manitoba. They were promised they would receive the same level of funding as comparable provincial agencies operating in the same field. Under the previous Government that did not happen and those agencies did not receive enough money to provide adequate training for their people.
The same problem exists today. The Awassis agency in northern Manitoba has been criticized by a government investigative group for not having an adequate training program. That is a result of the Government's own failure to provide the necessary funding. Mr. Speaker, the actions of the previous Government and this Government have resulted in a situation which hurts native people.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance. The Conference Board of Canada, a group that the Minister has often cited as being a reputable, independent minded forum for economic analysis, has put forward a study showing that Canadian taxpayers will be expected to carry an additional $4.6 billion debt, which will cause a substantial rise in the new sales tax being put forward by the federal Government. Mr. Gilles Rheaume, Director of Forecasting, said: "To cover the revenue shortfall due to the free trade agreement the rate of the sales tax will likely be higher than would otherwise have been the case".
I want to draw to the attention of the Minister and the House that the Minister of Finance has never been honest or forthcoming with the Canadian taxpayers about what the cost of the trade agreement would be. The Conference Board is saying that it would be an additional $4.6 billion per year and that that will cause a substantial rise in the sales tax.
When will the Minister be honest in the House and tell Canadians exactly what the real cost to them will be in additional raises in the sales tax to cover the cost of this misbegotten trade agreement?

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT CONFERENCE BOARD ANALYSIS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think what I have said in the House on this issue and on other issues has been very direct, very forthcoming and, to use the Hon. Member's words, very honest in presenting the facts to the Canadian people about economic policy and the effects of economic policy.
I have read Mr. Rheaume's analysis. I have only seen it in the newspapers this morning. However, one thing that the Conference Board analysis has not covered, at least according to the newspaper article I have read, is the impact of the trade agreement on economic growth. Every credible economic study on the free trade agreement has said that there will be increased economic growth. That is the way we are going to pay for any loss of tariff revenues. People will be getting lower prices. Their purchasing power will be increasing. Investment activities will increase.
Let me draw the Hon. Member's attention to what is happening today as we see all around us investment activity, investment intentions at very high levels, in the order of 15 per cent to 20 per cent this year. It looks like it will continue into next year as well.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I want an answer to my question. According to Agro Business and many farmers' organizations in Canada, 150,000 jobs would be lost in Canada's agricultural sector and the free trade agreement would be a disaster for Canada's farmers. Can the Minister confirm the figures indicating that workers in Canada's agricultural industry will lose 150,000 jobs, and is he now ready to renegotiate agriculture in the free trade agreement?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Minister responsible for Privatization and Regulatory Affairs; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: FREE TRADE AGREEMENT WITH UNITED STATES-REQUEST FOR RENEGOTIATION BY GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member is acting like a cowboy who, for all his life, has never stepped in cow manure.
Quite frankly, those types of questions are clearly an insult to the farming community. Farmers know that the McCain food organization is not the best representative of the farming industry.
The Economic Council of Canada conducted a study and predicted that there would be a net increase of 2,100 to 6,400 jobs in the food processing sector as a result of the free trade agreement.
Yesterday the Minister for International Trade went through the list of agricultural organizations from coast to coast that support the trade initiative. Some of them are right in the Hon. Member's backyard.
September 16, 1988

The Minister certainly seems to know a lot about cow dung, Mr. Speaker. I want an answer from this Minister on behalf of the farmers of Canada. This advertisement is sponsored not only by McCain Foods but by the Ontario Federation of Agriculture, the Nova Scotia Chicken Marketing Board, the Union des Producteurs Agricoles du Quebec, and they are all reputable farm organizations.
Will the Deputy Prime Minister admit today that those people are accurate when they say that 150,000 jobs will be lost in the agri-business and farming industry because of the trade deal between Canada and the United States? Will the Deputy Prime Minister answer yes or no?

speakeroldname: Hon. Charles Mayer (Minister of State (Grains and Oilseeds)):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, let me answer the question as a farmer. I talk to farmers, I live on a farm, and I farm. My neighbours are farmers. They realize that Canada produces some of the best quality agricultural products in the world. This deal will produce opportunities for us to sell.
The reason we will be able to sell, be successful, and produce additional jobs, is because we in Canada are good at what we do. We will be able to show, in the United States, that we are good at what we do when we are able to sell there under better rules.
The Canadian Canola Council has stated that it can see the possibility of an additional two million acres of Canola in western Canada which will be needed to supply the demand in the United States. The Canadian Cattlemen's Association accounts for 20 per cent of all the agricultural products produced in this country. They support this deal. The hog association supports it. We have a $2 billion hog industry that is in favour of free trade.
I would suggest to the Hon. Member that he talk to some farmers and find out what is really going on.

Canadians would like to know whether the statement made by the Prime Minister last week on the environment is an electoral move, or a deeply felt conviction. Is the Deputy Prime Minister in a position to commit the Government, in light of the general statement made by the
Oral Questions
Prime Minister on the environment, to pay the one-third share of the cost of rebuilding and reconstructing sewers on which depend the quality of our water, our health, and our beaches?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Minister responsible for Privatization and Regulatory Affairs; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am interested to note that the Liberal Party has released a policy paper on the environmental issues of the day.
I wonder where it was 10 years ago, particularly the Hon. Member who was the Minister of the Environment just over four years ago. He seems to be an expert on it today, but he certainly did not know much about it then. The fact of the matter is that what we have here is the Liberal Party making policy on the run. Let us look at the record.
We have provided $150 million to assist in the clean-up of large emission sources; $42 million loan to Noranda; provided $25 million to assist companies with the development of new technologies; $90 million to a world-class acid rain research institution; reduction of allowable emissions; and the clean-up of the St. Lawrence. There have been a number of initiatives.
When we came into office there were no specific emission control plans. There was no financial assistance to develop needed pollution control technologies.

subtopic: REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT ALLOCATE FUNDS FOR SEWERS
REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT ALLOCATE FUNDS FOR SEWERS
speechtext:

My supplementary question is the following. To demonstrate the commitment of the Prime Minister to Canadians and to the environment, and more important, in order to be credible in the eyes of Canadians, will the Government, instead of allocating funds for submarines, allocate funds for sewers?

September 16, 1988
Oral Questions FORESTRY

Mr. Speaker, my question is also directed to the Deputy Prime Minister. Yesterday the Prime Minister made what is clearly a deathbed repentance in appointing a Minister of State for Forestry. This comes despite the savaging of the shakes and shingles industry with a 35 per cent export tax, and the softwood lumber dispute which was bungled by the Trade Minister who had other fish to fry.
If the Prime Minister was really serious-and I ask the Deputy Prime Minister the following question in all seriousness-why during the four years of this Parliament, if the protection and the enhancement of Canada's largest industry were so important, has a National Forest Act never been produced, tabled, or debated in the House and brought forward as law in order that the Minister of Forests had a mandate under which to operate?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Minister responsible for Privatization and Regulatory Affairs; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we said that we would establish a full-fledged Department of Forestry. One of the first things that we did when we came into office was designate a Minister of State responsible for forestry. That is something that was never in place before.
We have continued working with the provinces in developing programs whether they be under ERDAs or under other specific programs. We have worked in co-operation with the provinces, because, as the Hon. Member knows, a large part of the jurisdiction remains in the hands of the provinces. It is a joint responsibility. However, the federal Government has taken leadership and is reaffirming that leadership by the designation of a full-fledged Department of Forestry.

Mr. Speaker, first, there is no National Forest Act and the Government has made no attempt to bring one forward. There has not been, and there still is not a Deputy Minister of Forests who can sit around the table and talk about cash. Canada's largest industry has received $609.9 million in forest renewal agreements during the tenure of the Government, which is the same amount received by the Reichmanns in the Tittle Egypt Bump from the Minister of Finance.
Why has the Government still not even given a mandate to negotiate, which I have confirmed in a letter from the junior Minister of Forestry, new forest development agreements with nine of the 10 provinces? It is a lot of bumf and you should know it, Mr. Deputy Prime Minister.

speechtext: What we have had here, especially from the NDP, is filibustering and blockading to the extent we had to sit all summer to get our legislative program through. Now they are asking for more legislation.

Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the newly appointed Minister of Housing I will address my question to the Deputy Prime Minister.
After four years of federal neglect of housing, after slashing and eliminating a variety of federal programs, and after ignoring the pleas to confront the crisis in affordable housing in Metropolitan Toronto and other urban centres, taxpayers expect the Government to do more than just engage in electoral cosmetics.
Rather than simply establishing another ministerial position on the eve of a national campaign, one which will not lessen the price of a home in Toronto by one nickel, why did the Government not respond by implementing real housing initiatives and programs for first-time home buyers in Toronto that would offer real solutions to the spiralling cost of homes which is rapidly making the dream of owning a home an impossible nightmare? When will the home buyers get the bacon rather than simply the sizzle?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Minister responsible for Privatization and Regulatory Affairs; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as was indicated in the House by the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister, housing starts are at record levels, up over 40 per cent. There have been in excess of
200,000	housing starts per year. Payments by individual mortgage owners have come down as a result of the decline in interest rates.
Today the newly appointed Minister of State for Housing is announcing in Toronto that 50 hectares of land at Canadian Forces Base Downsview in the Metropolitan Toronto area are being released, and this will provide up to 5,000 new homes and living accommodation for 10,000 to 12,000 people.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, the issue is not, as the Prime Minister said yesterday and the Deputy Prime Minister repeated today, housing starts. The crisis is in affordable housing. Toronto is becoming a playground for the rich and well-to-do. However, I welcome the fact that at the eleventh hour of the Government's life it has seen fit to release a number of hectares of land on the Downsview Air Force Base for affordable housing.
September 16, 1988

My question, though, is why has it taken four years, after repeated demands from Ontario and the Official Opposition, to release surplus lands for the construction of homes? Is this project simply an isolated case, or is the federal Government prepared to make a commitment that surplus federal lands in Metropolitan Toronto will be offered for housing projects on a priority basis to municipal and provincial Governments?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Minister responsible for Privatization and Regulatory Affairs; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is unfortunate that the Hon. Member prepared his question before listening to my answer. That is exactly what I said. Some 50 hectares of land have been released for 5,000 homes which will provide accommodation for 10,000 or 12,000 people.
The Hon. Member asked about a long-term commitment. The mere fact that we have appointed a Minister of State for Housing is a recognition of the difficulties in housing across the country, particularly in the Toronto region. That should be a clear signal of a clear commitment by the federal Government to take this issue seriously.
Of course, I remind the Hon. Member that there may be more announcements in the future, and he will be disappointed because the Official Opposition would rather we did not do anything so they would have something to criticize us about rather than giving us credit for what we are doing.

Mr. Speaker, my question is also directed to the Deputy Prime Minister. He talks about housing starts being up. That is fine for those making $80,000 a year or more. It does not help people at the low and middle-income level at all.
Over the last several years the Government has said no to every concrete proposal put forward to alleviate the housing crisis. Do the Minister and the Government think that simply appointing a Minister of Housing at this late date is going to convince Canadians anywhere that the Government is serious about providing affordable housing?

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto Jelinek (Minister of Supply and Services):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not know where the Hon. Member has been because the record of this Government speaks for itself.
Oh, oh!
That is the problem.

This Government has spent on average $1.5 billion a year on social housing, $250 million in the Metropolitan Toronto area alone. The fact is that the effort and commitment of this Government are now confirmed and solidified by the appointment of a Minister of State for

Housing. We are moving in the direction of providing additional social housing for senior citizens, the disabled, and affordable housing for young couples starting out.
The record of this Government speaks for itself and the solidification of that record will provide even greater opportunities for the needy in the housing area.

Mr. Speaker, I have been in the House and I have watched the Government slash funding for co-op housing, slash funding for social housing, and fail to follow through on commitments it made to all kinds of organizations for native housing, co-op housing, and social housing.
I ask whether or not this new Minister is going to carry through with the responsibility that any Government has to make housing a right rather than something that comes along on the eve of an election?

I am surprised that the Hon. Member is not applauding the efforts of this Government which is committed to making cheaper housing available to all Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Minister of Employment and Immigration I will direct my question to the Acting Minister.
As Canadians go to the polls, I think the single biggest blight on the Government's record has to be its treatment of those who cannot help themselves, such as older workers. The first thing the Government tried to do was cut back on seniors' pensions. The second thing it did was cut out any federal program for older workers. Older workers have been waiting two and a half years for the federal Government to reinstate some kind of program and plan to help them. I think it is a national disgrace that even though the recession ended years ago, older workers still have a higher rate of unemployment than they did before the recession ended.

September 16, 1988
Oral Questions
In the face of this absolute disdain for older workers, when there is one program which has been working, operating out of the Hamilton Help Centre, funded by an Innovations grant, why is the Government planning to cancel that program which has an 88 per cent success rate in returning older workers to work?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jake Epp (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one can notice that as the Opposition gets more desperate, the rhetoric from the Hon. Member, who we thought had reached the highest level of rhetoric, goes even beyond that. I want to tell her and other Members of the House that in the last four years the unemployment rate has gone down. About half a million people are out of poverty, and 1.2 million jobs have been created in four years. More than
700,000	of those jobs are for women. For example, the spouse's allowance was increased, the widow's allowance was increased, and veterans' allowances were increased.
The lousy child care program.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Child care is coming. I thank the Hon. Member for that tip. One could go on and on.

I would like to ask the Minister a very specific question. He talks about rhetoric. I have an independent analysis here done by a company which showed that the Hamilton Help Centre had established a program which cost $3,511 for each client and had an 88 per cent success rate. It put the Firestone workers back on the job. The savings to the Canadian taxpayers, according to an independent assessment, amounted to $18,342.45 per client.
Why is the Government throwing away a program that at a cost of $3,500 is sending older workers back to work, throwing them a lifeline? People do not want to be on welfare. I have letters from people who want to work and who have been given absolutely no hope by the Government. Will the Government reinstitute the program at the Hamilton Help Centre and make it a model for the whole country?

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Deputy Prime Minister. In 1985 the Secretary of State for External Affairs announced that a Polar 8 ice-breaker would be constructed to protect our Arctic sovereignty. Since then, British Columbia Members of Parliament and a number of cabinet Ministers repeatedly have promised that this ice-breaker would be built equally in Vancouver and Victoria, a measure which is desperately needed to save our shipbuilding industry. Since the Deputy Prime Minister has been actively interested in this, can he tell us when construction of the Polar 8 ice-breaker will begin as promised repeatedly over the last three years?

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto Jelinek (Minister of Supply and Services):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member should know that the Polar 8 is in its definition phase. There have been-and this is no news- some ownership problems with the company. The program and the plan is to continue to look forward to the Polar 8 icebreaker being built both in Vancouver and Victoria shipyards, and I believe that everything is going according to plan at this point in time.
Mr. Speaker, I must say that that is not the understanding we have on the West Coast. First, I understand there are financial problems because the Government underfunded this.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Start telling the truth, then, stop telling lies.

Second, we demand that this be built equally in Vancouver and Victoria. If there is a financial problem, why does the Government not increase the the subsidy? It really was underfunded, as I understand it.
September 16, 1988

Does the Minister not agree that a world-class ice-breaker which will do many practical things in our Arctic waters as well as deal with the sovereignty issue is far more important than wasting money on expensive nuclear subs? Let us have an election goody for Vancouver and Victoria.

subsubtopic: QUALIFYING PERIOD FOR RECEIPT OF BENEFITS-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Deputy Prime Minister. For at least another month, the qualifying period for unemployment insurance in Southern New Brunswick will be 16 weeks. Of course people in New Brunswick prefer to work all year round but they often have trouble finding even 10 weeks of employment. The Minister of Employment and Immigration has already indicated that she was looking into the problem, although it has already been given thorough consideration and she has all the information she needs to make a decision. My question to the Minister is this: How much longer will New Brunswick's workers have to wait for the Minister to make a decision to restore the 10-week qualifying period?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is addressed to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. The Government has been engaged in a flurry of activity in its last few days trying to convince the people of Canada that it keeps its promises. Among those who are supposed to be pleased by the appointment of a Minister of Multiculturalism are a great many looking to another promise the Prime Minister made before the United Nations on October 23, 1985, with respect to the imposition of complete economic sanctions on South Africa.
My question to the Secretary of State is simply this: Will the Prime Minister, when he goes to the United Nations on September 29, fulfil the promise made three years ago that Canada will now impose complete economic sanctions upon South Africa?

We believe there is some-

speechtext: Will the Prime Minister of Canada discredit Canada or disappoint those who fight apartheid when he goes to the United Nations? No, of course, he will not. subsubtopic: REQUEST THAT MINISTER MEET WITH UNIONS
speechtext:
