The House resumed consideration of Bill C-144, an Act to authorize payments by Canada toward the provision of child care services, and to amend the Canada Assistance Plan in consequence thereof, as reported (with amendments) from a legislative committee; and the amendments of Ms. Mitchell (p. 19310).

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: When I left the chair the Hon. Member for Skeena had two minutes remaining. Since he is not in the House, I will recognize the Hon. Member for Yukon.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to speak to this amendment because I believe it is one of the most useful amendments to this legislation. I want to use some examples to illustrate why I support the amendment very heartily since there must be a transition stage for the implementation of any new child care legislation.
Many of us believe that this particular legislation is so flawed that there is not much that can redeem it. However, I am pleased to speak to the proposed amendment that at least the Canada Assistance Plan be kept in effect during a transition period as we go into a new and hopefully improved child care Bill other than what is being proposed here.
The example that I think best illustrates why this is so necessary is the state today of child care services in the North, particularly for aboriginal people. Northern Canada is largely rural and therefore the child care services have been greatly underdeveloped. The problems in urban areas often relate to a lack of space, an extremely serious issue which this Bill does not address adequately. In rural areas there is simply no child care services available at all and virtually no resources in order to institute any child care.
What is needed in most of the rural areas is not just the funding that would be available under the Canada Assistance Plan or even under the proposed child care plan, but assistance to develop and institute child care services that are both
culturally appropriate and appropriate to the general lifestyles of the community.
The Inuit Women's Association, Pauktuutit, has given a very good submission to the committee. I think it underscores the problems that one sees in the North and in particular with aboriginal communities. The Inuit Women's Association points out quite well the need for culturally appropriate child care services. As you know, Mr. Speaker, the concern with child welfare services generally by aboriginal first nations has been one of very major paramountcy in discussions between the provinces and the territories and the federal Government, as well as within the communities themselves.
The history of child care services and child welfare services throughout Canada with first nations has proven to be an abysmally sad and abysmally ineffective one. Therefore we do not want to see that in instituting a national child care program those lessons from the past are not taken into account.
The Inuit Women's Association points out the need for culturally appropriate child care services. It is quite unclear whether in this proposed Bill there is enough flexibility to accommodate the kind of comprehensive community-based child care that would probably deviate from many of the southern models in order to meet the needs of those particular communities. This particular issue underscores the need for both a transition period through CAP and for rethinking of a number of the clauses of this Bill.
A second issue which very much underscores concerns with this Bill has been raised in particular by the Yukon Child Care Association. At the moment it is made up of a number of commercial operators. They have been adamant as an association that child care must not be a commercial venture, that it must be non-profit. As an association it supports this principle.
When looking at northern services or aboriginal services, the Inuit association again underscores the point that the profitmaking commercial centres to which much of the child care Bill is directed to support meet the needs in the North but will not meet the needs of aboriginal communities. Child care standards, trained staff, and so on are extremely difficult in the Yukon, the Northwest Territories, and I am sure in many of the northern parts of the provinces. If this is a problem in the South we certainly see that it is exemplified 10 times in the North.
This child care Bill which puts such a strong focus on commercial operations will not in our view in any way meet the needs of the North. Obviously, if commercial operations would have been viable they would be operating now in many of the remote and isolated communities. Clearly, that is not cost effective for them. However, the children in those spaces are no less important. They will run the communities in the future. They are just as important.
September 16, 1988

Another issue I would like to address in relation to this amendment concerns the question of training. This is a particular problem for us in the North. It is a particular problem in developing the kind of training programs which, as I said earlier, are culturally relevant and which meet some of the special needs of northern communities. I give as an example the fact that many aboriginal people whom I know in small communities throughout the territories are eager to seek retraining and upgrading of their skills. Very often the problem is that there is simply no child care available for them. There is no way for them to take the courses which may be available in order to provide a better standard of living for their families. Therefore they are forced to remain in the condition they are in even though they are being told by other Departments of the Government that these programs are available, that they want to see people upgrade their skills, that there are opportunities and jobs out there. At the same time they are being limited because there is simply no child care available and no provision for them to receive it.
Introducing a Bill such as this will have particularly serious repercussions for many of the rural communities across the country, in particular northern and more remote communities. This is why national standards are so important to those of us in the North. We know that with the small population base we are not often in a position to provide the numbers which count for commercial viability. Therefore non-profit centres and national standards which include provisions for well trained staff, both in terms of cultural relevancy as well as in terms of child care methods more appropriate to the dominant population, are things that we look to in a child care Bill to ensure that all the children in our North receive the care that we expect in southern Canada which will enable them to be the citizens of the North that we feel that they can and will be.
The Inuit Women's Association petition in many ways simply reflected many areas of concern that other groups have. It exemplifies the very basic rationale for the amendment which is before us now.
Therefore I strongly urge that this amendment be supported by all Members of the House. If we are to have a national child care Act which truly meets the objectives of caring for the children of the country, then it is important to ensure that nothing is lost in the interim through having the Canada Assistance Plan terminate before a full-fledged national program is in operation.

Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that it is important for the House and for our country that we correct some of the comments that have been placed on the record today and yesterday by members of the Opposition concerning this Bill. The Bill before us is a national child care Bill. It is aimed at doubling the number of subsidized day care spaces in the country over the next seven years. It has been implied and statements have been made many times that in some way, shape, or form this Bill will actually reduce the
Canada Child Care Act
number of potential day care spaces that will be provided in the country.
It is important that we bear in mind the distinction and the definitions of what we are talking about here. There is something in the day care industry called licensed day care spaces. As well, there is something called subsidized day care spaces. They are not exactly the same thing. There may be all sorts of children in day care and there may be all sorts of spaces for them as long as their families can afford to pay for the complete cost of that care. However, those spaces will be provided and there will be no subsidy provided for them, whether it be by the federal Government under the Canada Assistance Program or whether it be by the provincial Governments.
The spaces that we are really talking about here are the subsidized spaces. If we look to the situation in 1987, for instance, I am told that across the country there were some 243,545 licensed day care spaces. Of those about 180,000 were subsidized. Under the present provisions of the Canada Assistance Program there is no definition of what a subsidy is supposed to be, and therefore the subsidies could vary. Technically they could vary, I suppose, from a cent a day up to an enormous amount.
I am also advised that the subsidies vary substantially from province to province. Because there is no standard definition when we talk about 180,000 subsidized day care spaces in Canada at the present time, we are including in that figure spaces which are subsidized by provincial Governments in amounts as low as 38 cents a day, some as low as 50 cents a day, and some as low as $1 a day.
This Bill provides a standard definition for subsidized spaces that will require a subsidized space to provide at least a bear minimum subsidy of $2 a day. We are making a very significant change in the whole definition, in the whole concept of subsidized day care. I hear the Opposition talk about this business of not providing for those who are needy, for those who need assistance and help. In fact this legislation is doing just that; it is providing a much higher level of subsidization and guaranteeing a much higher level of subsidization for those people than is available now under the Canada Assistance Plan where this no minimum subsidization definition. That in itself is a very substantial step forward.
The other criticism I hear is of private day care centres or so-called commercial day care centres. There seems to be an impression that there is something sinister, vicious, and wrong with a private or a commercial day care centre. In fact, they have existed in Canada for a long, long time. Not only have they existed in Canada for a long, long time, they provide subsidized spaces. Many of the spaces in those commercial centres, in those private day care centres, are subsidized.

September 16, 1988
Canada Child Care Act
Oh, oh!

If the Hon. Member will listen to me for a minute, I will tell her that within my own block where I personally live in the City of Toronto there is a privately owned day care centre. There are subsidized spaces in it and it has been there for years. There are many, many more in my own neighbourhood.
Read the studies.

Of the 243,545 licensed day care spaces in Canada in 1987, some 90,386 were in so-called commercial centres or private centres. Of those 90,386, 54,000 of them or 60 per cent were subsidized spaces. This is not something new that is suddenly coming on the scene. The Government is not creating some sort of sinister plot to destroy day care and to destroy the whole system or to change things in a cruel and vicious manner. This is just carrying on the system that has been there for years and years.
If we listen to the comments of the Opposition and what they are suggesting and take them to their logical conclusion that somehow or other we have to wipe out those 90,386 private spaces, wipe out the 54,000 subsidized spaces in those private centres, and start from scratch with non-profit ones, it does not make any sense at all. If what we are interested in is providing day care for families that need it, then there is no point in wiping out what is there and having to replace it with something else. We should all bear these points in mind when we are dealing with this Bill.
Finally, I think that we should bear in mind that there is no provision for capital funding whatsoever under the Canada Assistance Plan. There is in this Bill-and it is one of the big improvements provided by this Bill and by this national child care legislative package-capital funding to allow more day care centres to be built, to allow them to provide extra spaces than there are now, and to provide extra subsidized spaces than there are now. That is what we are talking about, in fact doubling those numbers of subsidized spaces. That is the important and significant. That is why this Bill is so important to our country, as far as I am concerned. It is important to Canadians.
Thousands and thousands of people need day care. They cannot afford to pay for the whole thing themselves. They need some assistance and help if they are going to be working. Many, many single mothers, single parents, if they are going to be working and off the welfare and social assistance rolls, need some sort of subsidized day care space to allow them to do that. I think it is in the national interest to make sure that everybody who wants to work and does not want to be on social assistance has that opportunity. This legislation is geared to that very thing.
Most definitely, the impression that the Opposition has been leaving is that it will not meet that need. In fact, in the next seven years this legislation will double the number of subsidized day care spaces in Canada, and that is something for which the Government and the Minister should be commended.

Mr. Speaker, in addressing this amendment which seeks to prolong the assistance from the Canada Assistance Plan to Canada's day care consumers, I believe that I should start by paying tribute to the efforts of my colleague, the Hon. Member for Vancouver East (Ms. Mitchell), who has been our Party's chief spokesperson on the matter of day care.
I am glad to see that there is a minimal level of consensus in the House on the need for a national day care program for Canada. I, of course, must support my Party's program, which I see as being far better in addressing the real needs inherent in day care situations than the program that the Government has put before us.
The Government first became involved in day care through the operations of the Canada Assistance Plan, and I believe that it is inappropriate at this time for that involvement to be discontinued. That, of course, is by way of subsidies for the children of parents who were receiving social assistance to enable them to attend day care while their parents were seeking work or simply taking care of other major family responsibilities. That help for low-income parents enabled many children to have their start in day care in all parts of Canada, and I believe that it is significant that we now have an amendment to continue that participation.
If there is not a transition period for the continuation of Canada Assistance Plan funding, a risk exists that some children might not receive the day care services that they require and otherwise would receive.
We believe that day care has to be universally accessible without regard to the income levels of the parents, and this is one way in which that assurance could be given to those people who are receiving social assistance.
The present program as laid down by the Government in fact implicitly acknowledges that the demand for day care in Canada will continue to outstrip the supply and that indeed the gap between the demand for day care services and the availability of day care spaces will even widen, in terms of absolute numbers, if this amendment is not adopted and the Canada Assistance Plan funding continued.
For this country to fall behind the growth in demand for day care services, in spite of a child care Act and a supposed national program, would be an insult and a disservice to those parents who are seeking day care for their children in this day and age.
September 16, 1988

We in our Party believe that day care should be provided on a not for profit basis, notwithstanding the remarks of the previous speaker. Indeed, I would hearken back to the remarks of my colleague, the Hon. Member for Yukon (Ms. McLaughlin), in instancing the wide support is even among commercial day care operators for a not for profit situation.
I was not personally at the hearing concerned, but I was struck by the submission that was made by the Assembly of First Nations to the committee on Bill C-144. The Assembly of First Nations has correctly identified a problem that is not simply a problem of jurisdiction but one that has very far-reaching implications for the first nations and for their Governments at the band level in Canada.
It would be a sad day for this country if in, instituting a national day care program, purportedly anyway, this Government did not make the appropriate adjustments to ensure that first nations have full control within the federal guidelines, and hopefully the national standards which we would like to see instituted, over the delivery of day care programs to their first nations' citizens in their first nations' communities.
To place apparently unthinkingly, or without adequate consideration, the first nations of this country under provincial jurisdiction in the matter of day care programs would run completely counter to the self-government trend, and the development of self-government which has been occurring in aboriginal communities across the country and which has been, ostensibly at least, supported by all three Parties represented in the House. Therefore, I would charge the Government to ensure that no such derogation from the rights of first nations' communities to determine the framework under which these services are delivered should be accomplished by this legislation.
Aboriginal communities are of course among those which would be most severely affected by the withdrawal of Canada Assistance Plan funding because of the slender income base of many of those communities. I think of the communities, for example, of Whitefish Bay and Shoal Lake in my own riding with successful day care programs in operation that are facing certain needs. Certain resources have to be provided if those programs are to continue to succeed. Where will they be if this withdrawal of Canada Assistance Plan funding goes through.
Another question brought before the committee, which I think is certainly worthy of consideration and requires careful attention in the addressing, is the matter of training for those who serve in day care centres. Child care has become a feminized profession, and unfortunately it has joined other feminized professions in exhibiting the characteristics of underpayment of the workers, the caregivers within the profession. That is something that I would have liked to have seen addressed in the legislation because it is a fundamental equity issue between persons of the female gender and persons of the male gender that has not been adequately addressed by the Government. We certainly would hope to see it addressed much more forcefully by the next Government.
Canada Child Care Act

Mr. Speaker, last night I had the privilege of taking part in a program on CHOT to discuss the issue of day care and its potential impact on the election campaign. Mr. Speaker, I assume that during the coming election campaign, all Parties will put before the Canadian public their respective programs for setting up day care centres and providing for child care services. Mr. Speaker, I suggest we let the election campaign be the forum for the debate on major issues, including child care services.

Mr. Speaker, this is our last amendment that has been accepted for debate, although there are many others that we presented in a sincere attempt to find some way to improve this Bill since the Minister is determined to go ahead with it. Unfortunately, this Minister has refused almost all amendments except very minor ones.
This particular amendment relates to the Canada Assistance Plan. I would like to say that we have tried through three different amendments to deal with this problem. Through amendments we tried to get the Canada Assistance Plan retained for families in need, or those likely to be in need, for head start programs, and many of the services that are for low-income families now funded or those under the Canada Assistance Plan. We knew the Minister was balking at that, as is his want. We presented another amendment which would at least have kept children with special needs and disabled children under Canada Assistance Plan to ensure that those children have the type of spaces necessary, and that there is opportunity for them to have the subsidies needed to get into child care services.

Canada Child Care Act
It costs a lot for children who are disabled because there has to be special facilities. There should have been a top up per space that the Minister had in his funding formula to allow day care centres to have a certain number of spaces for disabled children in order that all centres would be accessible. This is a requirement under our Charter of Rights. The Minister has made no provision in this Bill to focus on and target the needs of disabled children. There should also have been money to pay so much extra per space for the extra costs for staff. Children with special needs need more attention, often one-on-one care. They should be integrated with other children in a day care centre.
When we had our special committee on child care we heard from witnesses that they did not want handicapped children to be isolated. It is very important that those children have a chance to develop normally. It is important for the other children to see there are members of our society who are disabled in one way or another. Many of us are disabled in other respects. We wanted to ensure that there was going to be a place for them in good quality child care services that their parents could afford in order that they could grow and develop in their pre-school years and have the socialization and stimulating intellectual experiences that would help to prepare them for school and to go on to make a success of their lives.
I am very sorry to say that this Minister refused to consider any mechanism within his funding policies and procedures to protect spaces for disabled children and for children with special needs. Many of the witnesses, in fact most, who appeared before the legislative committee said they wanted the Canada Assistance Plan operating here to be sure of protection for lower-income families and the programs and services parents and children need.
We talk about a child care Act. When the committee met we, including government Members, talked about families. We wanted child care programs to meet the needs of mothers and fathers as well as children. This Bill does not allow funding for programs like the Mom and Tot program which the YWCA sponsors. That is classified as a recreation program and this Bill excludes it. Yet those kinds of programs are very important for mothers at home so they can get out for some relief, some fun, to talk to other adults, and of course so their children can have a pre-school experience. A similar kind of service is needed for immigrant women and their children to orientate themselves to Canada, to practise the language and get out in the community as well as to provide good child care.
This motion, then, is very similar to the last one. It would amend the Act to allow CAP to be used by provinces and protect primarily low income families while the new Act is established. The new Act would then provide capital funding and should certainly provide operating costs directly to day care centres and other child care services. They could then pay decent wages to their staff and reduce their fees to make the service affordable. The Minister talks about affordability in his preamble even though he would not agree to state that as
September 16, 1988
an objective in the Act. Yet there is no way this Bill really will guarantee affordable child care. It just entrenches the present system of unaffordable child care and poor quality child care across the country.
By keeping CAP in place there will be protection for low income families because the funding is continuous. It is not capped at the end of seven years. It would allow the other spaces to be used for average families and any child that needs it, and there would not have to be a competition for spaces. We are afraid that in our provinces most of the available spaces- there are few of them and they are of poor quality-could be used just for kids with special needs if the funding was such as to allow it. Yet there are other children, of course, that should be covered under general funding to day care centres. The Minister is here today and we ask him to accept this amendment so that CAP funding will be available while there is a phase-in of the new Act.
I would also like to point out that there are certain programs that can be covered under CAP which are very important. We should have them in every community. I am talking about Head Start, for example. That program was initiated in the U.S. and research has shown that as a result of very intensive enrichment programs for children who are quite seriously disadvantaged, most of them poor, it is possible to help them prepare for school and give them the kind of language skills they need to obtain more cultural enrichment programs. They can get the kind of individual attention and growth they need in order to be prepared for kindergarten and so on. This is vital. If they do not get it, they will be the drop-outs, they will grow into illiterate adults, and we know what a serious concern that is today.
We heard from researchers who looked at Head Start programs. They found that children who had been through those programs had a much lower incidence of delinquency when they became adolescents. There were fewer teen-age pregnancies and a higher participation in school because of fewer drop-outs. The Minister is depriving communities of that by this plan and by not protecting funding for special programs for disadvantaged children.
Again, we have to really look at this Bill in the context of the needs of children across this country. We heard over and over again about children in every part of Canada who are in risky situations. The mother has to go to work and she does not have day care available in her community, or the fees are so high that she cannot afford it. All she can do is hope to heck she can find a baby-sitter, often someone she does not know, whom she can afford so she can go to work. Then she goes to work and worries about it all day long. This is not an unusual situation. It is particularly common for parents who have an infant child because there is no licensed, good quality care for under three-year-olds in almost every community, certainly not in my riding of Vancouver East. This is a constant complaint. It costs more for infant and toddler care, and it has to be good care.
September 16, 1988

We are also concerned about parents who have special needs. They want to be sure their children are cared for in a good centre. We are concerned also about the fathers who so often want to exercise their responsibility. Younger fathers are taking a greater share of the parenting and they want parental leave to do this. They will of course be just as worried as the mothers that their children are not in good care during the day simply because it is not available and not affordable.
I repeat, this Bill will not ensure accessible, affordable, quality child care in any one of our ridings across this country. It will not do that even though the Minister keeps trying to tell us that it will. This is not a national program. It has no objectives. It entrenches the present patchwork of low quality child care and commercial child care. There are too few spaces, only 200,000 for two million kids whose parents are working. Not all of them will need care, of course, but many of them will.
The program is very restrictive. It limits the expansion of child care to meet real needs. Capital funding will be finished after seven years. It will be grandfathered after seven years. I think the Minister should be grandfathered. He should be ashamed to be the Minister of National Health and Welfare with this kind of program. The women of Canada are not going to forget. They are aware of what is going on and we will make sure they are aware. The Minister has this last chance to improve the Bill by agreeing to this amendment, and I appeal to him again to do so.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to support the motion presented by the Hon. Member for the New Democratic Party. We have said repeatedly during the last few days that more than one million children do not have access to day care. We know that one child out of five is poor in this country, that 45 per cent of couples with children both have to work because they would otherwise live under the poverty line, and we know that the majority of single-parent families headed by women live below that line. When we look at this picture, we realize that we are faced with a major social problem. When the Minister says that families have a choice, it is clear he is not looking at the situation in 1988 and 1990, because families do not have a choice. Most families live below the poverty line. In this Bill we see that children from low and middle-income families have very little protection except for one amendment we managed to get through. However, the Bill does not address this particular group, and it is clear that today, a Bill as important as this one on child care must provide spaces for the groups that need them most, the children from low and middle-income families.
Of course the CAP program used to protect these children. In fact, one of the reasons why we support the recommendation that this program should be continued under the new legislation as well, is that we now have a ceiling. The number
Canada Child Care Act
of spaces is set. If we add the CAP program, it would focus specifically on these children and it would be a way of getting more spaces in the program.
Of course when we take a closer look at Bill C-144, we see it falls short in many respects. And speaking of lower and middle-income families and poor children, there was a week-long series of articles in La Presse on a study of the declining birth rate in Quebec. It appears that one of the causes is of course the cost of living but also the fact that women work. In fact, our recommendations included family support programs, one of which would provide for parental leave, not just maternity leave but parental leave. The Government ignored every single recommendation. It did not even propose an amendment to extend maternity leave from 16 to 26 weeks. Sixteen weeks is just not enough. That recommendation was made by all Royal commissions and all parliamentary committees, starting with the Royal Commission on the Status of Women in the seventies. The Bill contains nothing in this respect.
This Government always says we must do everything to help families, and that during the past four years it has passed legislation that might boost the birthrate, but if we look at paternity and maternity leave, they are not mentioned in the Bill. We discussed day care centres, including day care in the work place. Here again, not a trace in the Bill. If parents are to have a choice, they should have day-care available in the work place as well. Consider the problem of absenteeism. And it would be so much easier to get fathers involved, because we all know that bringing up children, although there have been some changes in recent years, is mainly the mother's responsibility. Here, fathers could at least be involved by bringing the children and picking them up. Companies could be given incentives such as tax rebates to provide this service. However, nothing of the kind was suggested by the Government.
We talked about special leave. We recommended special leave for parents. I think it is important to have a certain number of days a year, for when the children are sick and someone has to stay home to look after them. There is no mention of that either. It is clear that in addition to helping families, if these recommendations had been followed up in the legislation, they would also have helped to boost the birth rate in this country. It is all very well to tell couples to have more children, but there is more involved than that.
Mr. Speaker, parents are not involved in day care, but they still have a role to play. We know that even private schools and colleges have a board made up of parents who participate, who want to know the kind of services offered, the kind of education their children are receiving. But now, in day care centres, the children do not have a say, they are too young and the parents will not be involved in the quality of services, the selection of those who look after their children. Parents are completely excluded. I think that we could have had private day care, but insisted that parents be involved in running it.

September 16, 1988
Canada Child Care Act
As for the number of spaces, there are 200,000! This only meets 15 per cent of the present demand in Canada and we know that we are leaving more than 70 per cent of the population without day care service.
So many improvements could have been made, but I still support this motion because, coming back to CAP, we know that children with little education and whose parents are not very wealthy have almost no place in our society and now, from the beginning, at birth, there will be a cleavage. We might easily find ourselves with two societies, one rich and one poor. We will then have two classes of children as we have two classes of citizens. It is unacceptable in a country like ours, Mr. Speaker!
Every child in Canada is entitled to a space in a day care facility, to quality child care. Now, I must admit that the Bill before us does not give them many possibilities.
Someone just said that the workers in day care centres were mostly women. The pay is so low that they do it out of a sense of vocation, because we know that in some places they earn between $10,000 and $13,000 a year. So if you have to look after a family-only women can continue to take care of a family on such a low salary, whereas for men, it is twice as difficult-
So let us say that I support this amendment because I think that it is important to give our children-especially since one in five of them is poor in Canada-another chance to have the same day care services, just as the same education services, to get them out of the bad situation in which they have lived. A society like ours, Canada with all its wealth, must give, and has a duty to give, every child what it needs to get ahead in life. Later, it would be easier to say that we want programs to deal with delinquency and drugs, but at least, when they are young, we will give them what they need.
Unfortunately, I find that this Bill does not help families much and does not meet the real needs.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Debate.

Mr. Speaker, in addressing Bill C-144 again today, as I did yesterday, I must say that the more one looks at this Bill, the more one notes the deficiencies in the Bill and the lack of clarity and direction. This Bill is supposed to address children 14 years old and under, which is a very diversified group. At the same time, the Bill does not clarify how we handle these children, what kind of programs we have for these children. It does not address the issue of special need children.
Think about the number of children out in society. There are an additional 1.8 million places needed. We are serving two million children. Of those two million children who are supposedly in need of care, what numbers are over pre-school care? Within that over pre-school care, from age 6 to age 13 or 14 years, how many need latchkey service and what is the nature of the latchkey service we wish to provide for these children? Is it in the school? Is it out of the school? Is it an enrichment program? Is it to help reintegrate children who have problems? Is it to address single-parent families? What is the program targeting with respect to the kinds of services we want to give children who are 6 to 13 years of age?
With respect to under age five pre-school children, we have infants and young children two to four years who have different kinds of needs. I can recall many years ago, in another life in another place, I was president of a very wonderful agency, the Neighbourhood House Services of Canada. It was a reception and integration service for preschool children, among other services it offered.
The reason I bring this to your attention, Mr. Speaker, is because we started within that service some incredible programs, head start programs, which looked after aphasic children, Down's syndrome children and cerebral palsy children and we were able, through a demonstration program, to show that these children could be integrated into the normal pre-school programs. That enabled two things to happen. First, it sensitized children and parents to the reality that these children exist in our society and have the right to be helped to
Canada Child Care Act
be part of society to the best of their potential. They are not total handicaps. As I have said many times, if we could see them for the things they could bring to society instead of the handicaps they supposedly have, we would be far ahead.
As we prepared those children and sensitized their families, we also prepared society to adjust to the kinds of programs for the disabled which have become a very critical part of our society. Again, we must look at the abilities of those disabled instead of their disabilities only.
What are we doing in this Bill to address those children? What are we doing to enable their parents to have a sense of being supported in the school or pre-school system? Are we going to have great differences across Canada? I travelled with the Member for Vancouver East (Ms. Mitchell) through British Columbia and up through the Yukon for a week, as well as with other members of the child care committee. We heard of the importance to the interior of British Columbia of the kinds of services about which I am speaking. We heard about the need to have teachers who were trained, not just 18 year olds with good hearts and strong muscles.
There is a need for educational programs which teach how to handle these children, how to help them talk and walk. I met one of the youngsters in the aphasic program who had been tagged aphasic. He is a graduate of McGill University and a brilliant young architect today. If he had not had that special program, and if his parents had not had the support and help within the family structure of that agency, where would he be today?
The Down's syndrome children can perform. The cerebral palsy children may have what is a perceived difficulty, but that does not mean their intellectual capacity has been damaged. If we do not have in place the kinds of programs that are going to help these children and their families, it is a crying shame. This Bill is far short of its mark.
I would like to speak about the mathematics of the situation for a moment. Supposedly under CAP we have 200,000 spaces, 15 per cent of the need. Under this Bill, we will have 200,000 new spaces over seven years, another 15 per cent of the need. That leaves 1.4 million or 70 per cent of Canadian children with no option or choice. That is the point. Many parents choose to stay at home, but there are many who do not choose to stay at home for a variety of reasons which I enunciated yesterday.
What caught my eye-and I addressed the Minister yesterday on the difference between the preamble and content in a Bill-is that the amendment the Minister has brought to the preamble is kind of laughable. It is political chicanery, in my view. In the first paragraph he says there will be at least
200,000	new spaces over seven years. In the third paragraph it will not exceed $4 billion for the said program, some of which is recaptured from the CAP payments the Minister is not going to make. And there will be differences.

September 16, 1988
Canada Child Care Act
Because there are no national standards, there will be good programs and bad programs. There will be good programs for rich kids and bad programs for poor kids, which will divide our society even more. That is very unhealthy for the future of Canada. The Minister has set at least 200,000 spaces, but not exceeding $4 billion, so he has already installed that incredible difference that can mark our society in the future. If we have good programs, it will take more dollars for those 200,000 spaces than if we have poor programs.
All in all, it seems to me that there will not be sufficient money if the 200,000 spaces are put in and we cannot spend more than $4 billion under this Bill, and we have to respect the way the Bill was drawn up. There is no reason then why we cannot keep the CAP process in place and supplement the kinds of things that fall, perhaps, under recreation or education, the kind of special programs that are fundamental to the well-being of this country such as head start programs.
I suggest that this amendment is a good directive to the Minister on how to put a decent program into place. We cannot go back to 20 years ago when I was a mother who chose to stay at home. That is not the reality of today's society. In many instances a family needs two working parents. In many instances in today's society families have one single parent, divorce being as prevalent as it is. The mother and the father or the divorced partners must get out and earn a living.
If the future is in the hands of our children, for goodness' sake take money away from the submarines or somewhere else and put it into good and proper child care, divided properly among pre-school, school, and after school.

Mr. Speaker, 1 appreciate the opportunity to put a few facts on the record in this debate because child care is one of the crucial areas of debate today and is an emergency need which must be met rapidly.
Before I comment specifically on the substance of the Government's program, I want to reflect a bit on what the Minister responsible for day care had to say about our home Province of Manitoba. I understood him to have left the impression that Manitoba was a laggard in day care, that the New Democratic Party in Manitoba had done less than one might expect from a New Democratic Party on day care. He did this in a couple of ways. He indicated that Manitoba has the lowest rate of growth of spaces. He also referred to the cost of spaces being higher.
This brings to mind the fact that when making a case, people often choose statistics on a selective basis. They do not throw light on the situation as much as presenting their point of view. I want to deal with the contention of the Minister that Manitoba has the lowest rate of growth in spaces.
The Minister did not tell us, for example, that Manitoba has a far greater number of spaces when compared to the neighbouring Province of Saskatchewan, which is being governed by a Conservative Party. If my memory serves me correctly, there
are something like 3,000 spaces in Saskatchewan and 7,000 in Manitoba. Therefore, it depends upon which statistics you quote.
The Minister referred to the cost of spaces being higher in Manitoba. If you are to have quality care, you have to pay for it. When it comes to children Canadians are willing to pay for quality care. They do not want to go on the cheap when it comes to day care. They want the job to be done properly.
I want to place a few statistics on the record of the New Democratic Party in Manitoba with respect to day care. From 1981-82 to the end of the New Democratic Party term, there was a 225 per cent growth rate in Manitoba in the number of child care spaces. The dollars rose from $8.5 million to $27.5 million in grants for spaces and subsidies to parents. Therefore, from 1981-82 until the last provincial election in Manitoba, there was an increase of 225 per cent in spaces and subsidies to parents. That record stands by itself.
When we last debated this issue, I pointed out a few facts about Manitoba. One was that the Manitoba Government increased funding for day care spaces to $11,200 from $6,500, a 72 per cent increase from the fiscal year 1981-82 to the fiscal year 1986-87. That is a very substantial increase.
To finish off with statistics, Manitoba, which has had an NDP Government over most of the last few years, has the highest per capita spending on day care. On a per capita basis we have the most child care spaces. On a per capita basis Manitoba spends the most and has the highest standards.
I hope that this puts to rest the notion that Manitoba, under the New Democratic Party in the last few years, was a laggard with regard to day care because the reality is that Manitoba was a leader in day care. That is not to say that more does not need to be done because more does need to be done. This brings me to the Government's program now before us.
I guess it is not surprising that I am not critical of the Government's program. I am a member of the Opposition and we do have the responsibility to critique that which the Government does. However, I want to point out on the basis of facts why a critical view of the Government's programs stands up to reason and not only to passion and Opposition posturing.
The first reason has to do with quality. When it comes to child care, we all want quality. In order to assure that quality, we need national objectives. We know that more and more children and more and more families are dependent upon day care. We know that children achieve their basic learning in the very early stages of their life. They learn how to relate to the world, how to value themselves, and what to expect from people. They learn the very basic strategies of how to deal with the world as young children. It is, therefore, very crucial what they learn in that period because that largely determines what happens to them throughout their life.

Therefore, quality is fundamental, yet this program has no national objectives. It does not set out a set of principles which the provinces will have to live up to in order to get federal money. It does not set out objectives which point out that we want our children well cared for, that we want to ensure that the quality of care they get is excellent, that we want to ensure that they are not shortchanged in any way. There is a vacuum in the area of national objectives.
Somehow the Government has forgotten that it is the Government for the nation and is responsible for providing leadership to the people of Canada. It has forgotten that it is not simply enough to hand out money to the provinces and tell them to set the objectives, design the program, and do what they want with Canadian children.
Ordinary Canadian families expect more of their federal politicians than for them simply to be a funnel for dollars to provincial Governments. They want them to provide leadership in the sense of providing for valid social needs, which day care is, and in identifying how those social needs will be met. The Government's program falls flat on its face with regard to the quality criteria because it has failed to set out any national objectives ensuring that we will have quality child care spaces.
Another aspect of the program is that the legislation before this House removes the reference to day care from the Canada Assistance Plan. The Canada Assistance Plan is a piece of legislation passed by the House of Commons, the objective of which it is to ameliorate the impacts of poverty, to give people a way out of poverty, and to help people who are living below the poverty line in this country.
If the Government is seeking to meet one social need, why does it take away from the other? Why, in its attempt to do something about day care, does it forget about poverty. That is the implication of this legislation. That is the implication of this.
Bill C-144 removes from the Canada Assistance Plan the reference to child care. It is stated in Clause 10 and reinforced in Clause 11. It states that the Canada Assistance Plan will no longer include the objective of alleviating poverty. By no longer making any reference to child care the Government is saying to heck with the poor.
In order to reduce poverty in this country and get people off welfare so they can make a contribution to society, they must have training. One of the social supports people need in order to get training is day care. That objective ought to remain in the Canada Assistance Plan. Day care for the poor ought to continue to be a priority because only then will they have the tools to climb out of the deep pit of poverty. This Government program fails when one considers it against the criteria of what it does for the poor.
Let us examine the Government's program from the perspective of day care spaces. People in my riding and people across Canada want day care spaces so their children will be well cared for. The Government's plan reduces the number of

day care spaces that otherwise would be available to Canadian families. The growth rate for day care under the Canada Assistance Plan was 15 per cent per year. According to our calculations, it will be 10 per cent per year under the Tory plan. That is a step back in terms of provision of day care spaces. The Government is turning a deaf ear to Canadian families who say they want day care.

speechtext:
That the Standing Orders of the House be amended by inserting therein the requirement that all official documents tabled or distributed in the House be in both official languages; and
That the Clerk of the House be authorized and instructed to print a revised edition of Standing Orders of the House incorporating the said amendment, renumbering as may be deemed necessary and making such technical and consequential changes as may be required.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to say a few words on the motion, because it is topical and because it follows the decision taken by this House some time ago, when adopting a new Official Languages Act, in which Section 8 provides that any document tabled in this House by a federal institution, whether the Canadian Government or an agency, shall be tabled in both official languages at the same time.
That section of Bill C-72 reads as follows: Any document made by or under the authority of a federal institution that is tabled in the Senate or the House of Commons by the Government of Canada shall be tabled in both official languages.
As I see it, Mr. Speaker, the point is that the House of Commons is responsible for its own Standing Orders and they must be amended by the House. It does not matter how many Bills we pass, the House has to make a decision and a provision such as the one suggested today must be added to the Standing Orders. This is why the second paragraph states that the Clerk of the House be authorized to print a revised edition of the Standing Orders incorporating the said amendment.
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of my motion is quite simple. Hon. Members will recall that the 1969 legislation had a provision which was the source of some difficulties. Here is the text of section 2 of the Bill adopted in 1969, Chapter 0-2 of the Revised Statutes of Canada: "The English and French languages are the official languages of Canada for all purposes of the Parliament and Government of Canada, and possess and enjoy equality of status and equal rights and privileges as to their use in all the institutions of the Parliament and Government of Canada." That is clear enough: English and French are the official languages of Canada for all purposes of the Parliament and Government of Canada.
Up until 1987-88 my personal experience has been that the Government always tabled official documents in both official languages. As a rule, parliamentary institutions and government agencies did follow this instruction and documents were tabled in both official languages.
September 16, 1988

Occasionally the Government is too fast off the mark and is obliged-let's be nice-to table documents in one official language only. I am thinking more specifically of the free trade Bill which was tabled in English only, to my mind a major breach of a policy that is supposed to respect both official languages. What I want to do is have the House make a joint decision to amend its Standing Orders and bring them into line with the new Act and the spirit of the new Act, so that from now on, the Government and federal institutions are obliged to table all documents in both official languages, so that neither language group is put at a disadvantage in its work here in the House of Commons. Now is that so hard? I may remind the House that this suggestion has been discussed at length and interpreted quite generously, I believe, but sometimes the spirit of the Act has been ignored, and that is why I want to ensure that the House officially assumes these statutory or quasi-statutory obligations.
Mr. Speaker, Hon. Members will recall that although the 1969 legislation contains in Section 2, which I read earlier, a provision that says Parliament should respect both official languages, the courts, on many occasions, and I could quote a number, starting with the Les gens de I'air and up to quite recently in New Brunswick-The court ruled that the Official Languages Act, 1969, was declaratory rather than executory, and Hon. Members will recall Judge Deschenes' judgment, and since it was declaratory, it was merely a statement of intent which means it had no "teeth". That is why the Official Languages Committee and the Legislative committee considering Bill C-72, in its wisdom, accepted and why the Government endorsed-In the final instance, the amendment 1 presented in committee was taken up by the Government and adopted here in the House only a few months ago as part of Bill C-72, so that now, any document tabled in the House must be tabled in both official languages.
Mr. Speaker, I just want to stress another important point, which I hope will convince Hon. Members of the importance of adopting this motion today. Bill C-72 was passed by the House of Commons and by the Senate or the other place, as I should say, and everything is in place.
Royal Assent has been given, and the Bill only has to be proclaimed to become law. This proclamation has yet to take place, and I understand the problems that may be involved. However, I may recall Section 111 of Bill C-72, passed on July 7 here in the House, and I believe, at the end of July here in the Senate, and Section 111 says, and I quote:
Coming into force 111. Subject to subsection 94(2),...
which deals with the administration of justice in the provinces

to be fixed by proclamation.
So there may be one or more proclamation dates.
The Bill contains fourteen parts, so the Government could proclaim certain parts of the Bill now and proclaim other parts tomorrow or a month later or a year later or God knows when! It is to avoid too much hesitation and keeping the House waiting for further directives from the Government that I am
Standing Orders
proposing today that the House should adopt this motion which, as was said earlier, is quite clear and to the point, namely that from now on, all documents tabled by federal institutions will be in both official languages.
Mr. Speaker, this is not a very complex issue. I hope Hon. Members will be able to pass this motion quickly, and I want to thank them for their co-operation.

Mr. Speaker, my colleague tabled a motion that I think, at first glance anyway, is somewhat redundant. Perhaps it is because of his experience with this language issue, which has always been difficult in Canada, that my colleague has fears that, in some cases, have been justified. And maybe he neglected to do so, but he could have quoted Talleyrand, who said, "If it goes without saying, it would be better to say it!"
And the very purpose of his motion is to state once again that indeed "any document tabled in the House of Commons be in both official languages."
Nevertheless, I would like to remind my colleague, even though on this side of the House, I think, we will enthusiastically endorse this proposal, which is perhaps somewhat redundant, but which no doubt, in view of past experience, is useful and appropriate. So, for myself, Mr. Speaker, I will endorse this motion presented by my colleague from Ottawa- Vanier.
However, I would like to remind him that he should not use his prerogative as he did before when he was quite hard on the Speaker of the House after his own Party and the Opposition Parties had tabled nearly 130 amendments in only one of the two languages very late in the evening. You were quite hard on the Speaker of the House and, given the situation now at the end of the session when our clerks, translators and Hansard officials have an awful workload, it is impossible for them to deliver the goods on time. Mr. Speaker, I take this opportunity to pay tribute to our clerks, our translators and all those who work on producing the official record of our debates and do a tremendous job. The next morning, we see the amazing quality of what they do. How many times have I seen these workers, men and women who are professionals, come to see some Hon. Member and ask him to clarify what he meant, to make the necessary changes, to do a good job on our speeches, our debates and to do a good job too for the Canadian people who, from time to time, read what we say and listen to us!

September 16, 1988
Standing Orders
I would also like the Speaker of the House, who is responsible for this service, to look a little more closely into the working conditions of these professionals. Theirs is a painstaking job, like the work of the Benedictine monks. But I often feel that these latter-day Benedictines are less well treated that their predecessors in the middle ages were, because they have so much work to do, it is so demanding, so time-consuming, and especially at the end of a session. So the motion introduced by my colleague will mean additional work for those people who are at our service and at the service of all Canadians. Of course I would expect all Parties to co-operate. Perhaps it might be advisable and appropriate if they were to produce documents in both official languages before presenting them to the Speaker of the House. They ought to make every effort to assist the Speaker of the House and especially all those who are responsible for drafting legislation and amendments so as to speed up the debates and show respect for the spirit and letter of Bill C-72, and show respect as well for this country's linguistic duality which certainly ought to be most apparent in this House.
Mr. Speaker, I urge my colleagues to support the motion of the Hon. He would be welcome to negotiate with us, if he is so inclined. We do see the world similarly on many occasions, certainly when it comes to the importance of language policy.
My region is heavily dominated by people of non-francophone background. It is dominantly English, but there are Eastern Europeans, Asians, and people from all around the world. Lately, we are receiving more and more people from South America. Sometimes it is difficult for people raised in such a region to comprehend the reality that this has always been a bilingual nation. It has always been a nation with two languages spoken in the home that young children learn, and right from the beginning those two languages have been French and English.
Geographically that is spread around the country. In Newfoundland, the dominant language is English, and I believe that is clear. For most parts of Quebec, and some parts of northern New Brunswick, the dominant language is French. For the most part in western Canada the dominant language is English. If one is born into a dominant language region, sometimes it is difficult to understand why the country needs two languages. Sometimes I say to people in my riding that it does not; it is possible to separate it. It is possible to have two or more countries, one with an official language French, and one with an official language English. We could have that. There are people in political life who argue for that persuasion.
There is a political Party in the Province of Quebec that has formed a Government whose origin, in large part, was owed to the reality that it was difficult to be a Canadian. It felt difficult to be a Canadian if that person came from a region where the dominant language was French. It was not a comfortable feeling. I say to the people of my riding that if someone in the City of Calgary came along and said that all of our courts, all of our policemen, all of our businesses, all of our schools will force you to be French, the people would rebel. It would be easy to create a political Party that said we should separate and become a country with this official language we call English. That is a realistic political option, but for members of my Party it is a very undesirable option and, I suggest, it is so for the vast majority of Canadians.
We love this country called Canada. We do not want to see separation. If we are to prosper and stay united we have to recognize in legislative form and in our practices the reality of the duality of language in this country.
September 16, 1988

To come to the Member's motion, people in my riding will say why should any official document coming to the House of Commons have to be in both official languages? The answer is that if it comes to the table of the House of Commons and is distributed to me in this Chamber as your representative and it is in French, because I worked hard at the language I will understand it generally but I will not be able to understand it precisely. If it comes to me in English I can understand it precisely. If it comes to me in English but does not go to my colleague from Charlevois in French, then he will have trouble understanding it precisely. It is imprecision in understanding that lies at the heart of a lot of human quarrels. That is true of our own families in fights with our children or our spouses. They come about many times because we do not precisely understand each other.
When we come to the affairs of a nation, we have to work as hard as we can to make sure that we understand each other precisely. To do that we must have all of our official documents presented to us in the two languages. Those of us who learned French in our homes can understand the document in French, and those of us who learned English in our homes can understand the document in English. That is the importance and significance of that provision.
Bill C-72 provides us with that kind of fairness in our courts, in government services generally, in our workplace, and in our
Standing Orders
democratic processes. It is a magnificent advance on what we have had for the last 20 years. It is very consistent with statements made in this chamber on behalf of my Party by the Hon. Robert Stanfield on May 16, 1969, a 20-year commitment. It was a real pleasure in 1984 to finally get a majority that gave us the opportunity to implement the commitments made by Mr. Stanfield on behalf of all of us in the Conservative Party some 20 years ago.
